To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) a daily meal entrains circadian rhythms of activity in mice; (2) these rhythms require dopamine D1 receptors; and (3) these rhythms are sexually dimorphic.
1) a sex difference in the magnitude of food-anticipation is present in wild type mice and is amplified in D1R KO, and 2) D1 receptors in both sexes are important for food-anticipation.

(1) food-anticipating activity (FAA), the behavioral expression of a circadian food-entrainable rhythm, is sexually dimorphic in wild type mice and (2) the sexual dimorphism in FAA is amplified in dopamine D1 receptor knock-out (D1R-KO) mice.

the mechanisms that control circadian rhythms of behavior.

the dopamine D1 receptor is an important mediator of circadian entrainment by restricted feeding in mice, and that the D1R-mediated mechanism is sexually dimorphic.

there is a sexual difference in the circadian food-anticiapatory rhythms in mice.
